blocks.title: Buffer solution
blocks.text: Solutions that resist a change in their pH when a small amount of an acid or a base is added to them are called buffer solutions. They have a specific constant pH, and their pH does not change on dilution or on keeping for a long time.

Buffer solutions are mostly prepared by mixing two substances. Mixing a weak acid with its salt with a strong base gives an acidic buffer with pH less than 7; acetic acid with sodium acetate is one of the best examples. Mixing a weak base with its salt with a strong acid gives a basic buffer with pH more than 7; NH4OH with NH4Cl is one of the best examples.

Consider the acidic buffer of CH3COOH and CH3COONa. Acetic acid, a weak electrolyte, dissociates very little: CH3COOH(aq) + H2O(l) gives CH3COO-(aq) + H3O+(aq). When sodium acetate, a strong electrolyte, is added, CH3COONa(aq) gives CH3COO-(aq) + Na+(aq), the dissociation of CH3COOH is suppressed by the common ion effect of CH3COO-. As more CH3COONa is added, the added acetate decreases the dissociation of CH3COOH and the pH of the solution increases; the greater the concentration of acetic acid compared with sodium acetate, the lower the pH. blocks.text: A buffer of this kind is a large reservoir of CH3COOH and CH3COO-. When an acid (H3O+ ions) is added, the ions react with CH3COO- to give back acetic acid, so the pH remains almost unchanged, because CH3COOH, a weak acid, prefers to remain undissociated. Similarly the buffer of NH4Cl and NH4OH resists a change of pH and pOH when acid or base is added from outside. When a base (OH- ions) is added, the ions react with H3O+ to give back H2O and the pH again remains almost unchanged.
